segments.t: KorTTY protects your sensitive data with industry-standard encryption and centralized key management. All connection passwords, SSH key passphrases, and credential storage use AES-256-GCM encryption derived from a master password that is created on first launch.
On first launch, you are prompted to create a master password (minimum 6 characters) that encrypts all stored secrets.
Enter a password (the field border turns green when length is sufficient, red when too short).
A strength indicator shows password quality; a warning appears for weak or common passwords, but you can confirm if needed.
The master password itself is hashed with PBKDF2 (310,000 iterations) and never stored in plain text. The salt and hash are stored in KTPH000.

On subsequent launches, KorTTY prompts you to enter the master password to unlock encrypted data. Turning off KTPH000Require master password on startupKTPH001 in KTPH002Settings KTPH006 SecurityKTPH003 hides this prompt and starts with the vault locked: stored passwords and keys stay unavailable until you unlock it (see KTPH004Unlocking the vault laterKTPH005).

The second Security option, KTPH002Disable master password prompt on startup (auto-login)KTPH003, also removes the prompt but keeps the vault fully usable: korTTY writes your master password to KTPH000 — KTPH004obfuscated only, not encryptedKTPH005, with owner-only file permissions — and unlocks automatically on every start. The obfuscation key is embedded in the application, so file permissions are the only real boundary; anyone who can read KTPH001 or a backup can decrypt all saved secrets. On a brand-new profile the option bootstraps a default master password with no dialog at all. korTTY asks for confirmation before enabling it, it is meant for throwaway/test environments, and a KTPH006policy configurationKTPH007 that requires a master password disables it. Details: KTPH008Security settingsKTPH009.
If you lose the master password, encrypted data cannot be recovered. Delete KTPH000 and KTPH001, restart, set a new master password, and re-enter your passwords.

With the vault locked, choose KTPH000Configuration KTPH020 Security KTPH021 Unlock Vault…KTPH001 and enter the master password; the menu item is greyed out while the vault is open. Saving an AI or translation API key, a Hugging Face token, a jump server password or a Job Scheduler password, starting an AI Swarm run on servers without an open terminal, asking the guide a question and generating a single- or multi-server workflow script with an encrypted AI key show their "vault locked" message with an KTPH002Unlock Vault…KTPH003 button instead of a dead end. Connecting a saved connection whose password is stored in the vault, with KTPH004ConnectKTPH005 in the Connection Manager, a tab's KTPH006DuplicateKTPH007 or KTPH008Reopen Closed TabKTPH009, offers KTPH010Unlock Vault…KTPH011 as well; if you do not unlock the vault there, korTTY asks you to type the password instead (see KTPH012Signing inKTPH013). Opening a project while the vault is locked lists the tabs whose password is in the vault in the window's restore bar; unlocking the vault, with its KTPH014Unlock Vault…KTPH015 or any other way, opens them in every window (see KTPH016Tabs that wait for youKTPH017). Some places still only report the locked vault, for example an AI chat request or a key passphrase in the connection editor; unlock the vault from the menu first. After a successful unlock the action continues; KTPH018CancelKTPH019 leaves the vault locked without a second error. A wrong password keeps the dialog open, and cancelling it never quits korTTY.

Unlocking also restores the temporary SSH keys that could not be decrypted at the locked start; until then they stay stored encrypted, so saving connections in the meantime does not lose them. Windows that were already open while the vault was locked, such as the Connection Manager or the credential and key managers, do not pick up the unlock — reopen them to use stored secrets there.
All sensitive data at rest is encrypted using KTPH000AES-256-GCMKTPH001:
KTPH000Salt LengthKTPH001: 32 bytes (random per master password setup)
Each encrypted value combines a random IV with the ciphertext, encoded as Base64 for storage.
Store centralized username/password credentials that can be reused across multiple connections.

KTPH006Menu:KTPH007 Configuration KTPH020 Security KTPH021 Credentials… (KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013, on macOS KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019). The shortcut also works while a terminal has the focus.
KTPH000Password TypeKTPH001 — KTPH002Stored PasswordKTPH003, or KTPH004External CommandKTPH005 to fetch the password from a password manager (see KTPH006Passwords from an external commandKTPH007)
KTPH000EnvironmentKTPH001 — Production (the default), Development, Test, Staging, or one of your own (see KTPH002Environments and tab colorsKTPH003)
KTPH002Server PatternKTPH003 (optional) — Glob pattern (e.g., KTPH000, KTPH001) for automatic credential matching to connections

Instead of storing the password, a credential can fetch it from your password manager every time it is needed. Choose KTPH000External CommandKTPH001 as the KTPH002Password TypeKTPH003 and enter a command that prints the password, for example:
KTPH000Stored encryptedKTPH001 — the command itself is encrypted with your master password, like a stored password.

KTPH003ShellKTPH004 — the command runs in KTPH000 on macOS and Linux and in PowerShell on Windows, so on Windows write PowerShell syntax (KTPH001, not KTPH002). In the Flatpak package the command runs on the host, where your password manager's command-line tool is installed.
KTPH000OutputKTPH001 — the first line the command prints is the password. If the command exits with an error, korTTY shows its exit code and error output; empty output counts as an error too.

KTPH005No promptsKTPH006 — the command gets no input, so a tool that asks for a master password or PIN cannot be answered and fails at once. Unlock the password manager first, for example with KTPH000, or with KTPH001 and KTPH002 set in the environment korTTY was started from. The Flatpak package runs the command on the host without korTTY's environment, so there KTPH003 must be set in your desktop session, or passed in the command itself (for example KTPH004).

KTPH00010-second limitKTPH001 — a command that has not finished after 10 seconds is stopped together with every process it started, and korTTY reports the timeout. A Touch ID or system dialog the tool opens by itself must be confirmed within that time.

KTPH000Runs every timeKTPH001 — the command runs whenever the password is needed: when you pick the credential in the connection editor and whenever a connection that uses it connects. Panes split from a connected tab reuse that tab's password.
KTPH000TestKTPH001 — the KTPH002TestKTPH003 button next to the command runs it once and shows how many characters came back, never the password itself.

In the connection editor the password field shows KTPH000Retrieving password...KTPH001 while the command runs, and korTTY stays responsive. Opening, duplicating or restoring a connection waits for the command before it connects, for at most the 10-second limit, and the window does not react during that time; if the command fails there, korTTY uses the connection's own saved password or asks for one.
When creating or editing a connection:
Select a stored credential from the KTPH000CredentialsKTPH001 dropdown.
Username and password are filled in automatically; for an external command once it has returned the password.
The following diagram shows how credentials and SSH keys flow from encrypted storage to active connections:

Every credential belongs to an environment: one of the built-in Production, Development, Test and Staging, or one you add. KTPH000Environments...KTPH001 in the Credentials manager lists them; there you can add your own environments and rename or delete them. The built-in ones always stay, and an environment that a credential still uses cannot be deleted.

Any environment, built-in or your own, can have a KTPH000tab colorKTPH001: select it, tick KTPH002Mark this environment's tabs with a colorKTPH003 and pick the color. A terminal tab that signed in with a stored credential of that environment then shows the color as a dot in front of its title and as a frame around its terminal, just like a KTPH004connection's own tab colorKTPH005. Marking the Production environment red, for example, marks every tab that signs in with a production credential at once.
KTPH000Opt-inKTPH001 — no environment has a color until you pick one. New credentials start out in Production, so a default color would mark most tabs as production tabs.

KTPH000The connection's and the folder's color come firstKTPH001 — a connection with a tab color of its own shows that color, and a connection in a folder with a KTPH002tab colorKTPH003 shows the folder's, whatever environment its credential belongs to.

KTPH000Only credential-backed connectionsKTPH001 — the color reaches tabs that signed in with a stored credential, including a KTPH002teamworkKTPH003 connection that uses the team's default credential. Connections that log in with an SSH key, a temporary key or a password of their own have no environment; give them a tab color of their own, or color the Connection Manager folder they are in, instead.

KTPH000Applied on OKKTPH001 — color changes take effect when you click KTPH002OKKTPH003 in the Environments dialog, and KTPH004CancelKTPH005 discards them. Open tabs in every window pick up the new colors at once, as they do when you move a credential to another environment.

KTPH000Not by color aloneKTPH001 — pointing at a tab colored this way names the color and the environment, for example KTPH002Tab color: purple (#7B1FA2), from the credential environment LabKTPH003 for an environment of your own named Lab. Screen readers read the same text for the dot.
KTPH001Stored in KTPH000KTPH002 — together with your own environments; see KTPH003Configuration filesKTPH004.
KTPH000Environment-specificKTPH001 — Organize credentials by deployment environment
KTPH000Server Pattern MatchingKTPH001 — Automatically assign credentials to matching servers
KTPH000Encrypted StorageKTPH001 — Passwords are encrypted with AES-256-GCM
KTPH003Password managersKTPH004 — Fetch the password from a command such as KTPH000, KTPH001 or KTPH002 instead of storing it
KTPH000Automatic UsageKTPH001 — Select credentials directly in connection settings
Centralized management of private SSH keys with encrypted passphrases.

KTPH006Menu:KTPH007 Configuration KTPH020 Security KTPH021 SSH-Keys… (KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013, on macOS KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019)
Select the path to your private SSH key file.
(Optional) Enter the passphrase — it will be encrypted and stored.
KTPH000Centralized ManagementKTPH001 — Manage all SSH keys in one place
KTPH000Encrypted PassphrasesKTPH001 — Key passphrases are stored encrypted with AES-256-GCM

KTPH003Key CopyingKTPH004 — Use KTPH005Copy to User DirectoryKTPH006 to copy keys to KTPH000; on macOS and Linux the copied private key is made owner-only (KTPH001) and the folder KTPH002, and copied keys are included in encrypted backups and restored with owner-only permissions
KTPH001Wildcard SearchKTPH002 — Quick search for keys using KTPH000 patterns
KTPH000Automatic UsageKTPH001 — Select keys directly in connection settings
When creating or editing a connection:
Select KTPH000Private KeyKTPH001 as the authentication method.
Select the desired key from the KTPH000SSH KeysKTPH001 dropdown.
The key path and passphrase are filled in automatically.

Terminal and SFTP connections, including the SSH bootstrap used by Mosh, share a trust-on-first-use (TOFU) verifier keyed by normalized host name and port. On first use, korTTY displays the server key algorithm and OpenSSH SHA-256 fingerprint; verify it out of band before accepting. The confirmation defaults to KTPH000NoKTPH001. A previously trusted matching key is accepted silently, while a changed key is hard-blocked with the expected and offered fingerprints and is never retried or replaced automatically.

A changed key can be replaced only by an explicit decision, and only in a connection you opened yourself in a terminal tab or the SFTP manager (including its jump server). KTPH000Review and Replace…KTPH001 in the changed-key alert shows the trusted and the new fingerprint side by side; the replace button stays disabled until you confirm that you verified the new fingerprint with the server administrator, and KTPH002CloseKTPH003 and KTPH004CancelKTPH005 remain the default buttons. The replacement is a compare-and-swap: it is stored only while the trusted key is still exactly the one you reviewed, so a key changed in another window in the meantime is never overwritten. Every replacement is logged with the old and the new fingerprint. Background and restored connections, and the SSH bootstrap of Mosh, keep the plain block.

KTPH001Configuration → Security → Known Hosts…KTPH002 lists, searches and removes trusted keys. Removal works the same way: it deletes a key only while it still has the fingerprint shown in the confirmation, and the next connection asks again as on first use. With the enterprise policy key KTPH000, both replacing and removing are disabled, so only an administrator can change a trusted key.

Interactive pins are written atomically to KTPH000; a companion lock coordinates simultaneous korTTY processes. This store is distinct from the JobScheduler's connection-ID-based host-key pins in KTPH001, which protect unattended SSH, SFTP, and Rsync execution.

For lab or throwaway hosts you can turn the first-use prompt off and have korTTY accept an unknown key silently. This is an KTPH000accept-newKTPH001 relaxation, not blind trust: a key that differs from one already pinned for that host is still hard-blocked, so a man-in-the-middle on a host you have connected to before is still caught. It is off by default and can be set at three scopes, in precedence order:

KTPH000Per connectionKTPH001 — the KTPH002Host key verificationKTPH003 control in the Connection Manager's connection editor and in Quick Connect, with three states: KTPH004Use defaultKTPH005 (inherit), KTPH006VerifyKTPH007 (force strict even if the group or global setting relaxed it), and KTPH008Don't verifyKTPH009.
KTPH000Per groupKTPH001 — right-click a group in the Connection Manager and toggle KTPH002Disable host key verificationKTPH003; it applies to every connection in the group that inherits.
KTPH000GloballyKTPH001 — KTPH002Settings → Terminal → Disable host key verification for all connectionsKTPH003, the base default for every connection that inherits at both levels above.
A jump server's own host key is never relaxed by any of these — the bastion is always verified strictly.
Manage GPG keys for backup encryption and connection/snippet export encryption.

KTPH006Menu:KTPH007 Configuration KTPH020 Security KTPH021 GPG-Keys… (KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013, on macOS KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019)
KTPH000Manual EntryKTPH001 — Click KTPH002AddKTPH003 to enter key ID and email manually.
KTPH000System ImportKTPH001 — Click KTPH002Import from GPGKTPH003 to import keys from your system's GPG keyring.
Select a key from the list.
Click KTPH000EditKTPH001 to modify details, or KTPH002DeleteKTPH003 to remove.
Select KTPH000GPG EncryptionKTPH001 as the encryption type.
Choose the GPG key to use for encryption.

GPG-encrypted backups and exports are stored as KTPH000 files — a GPG backup as KTPH001 — and need your system's KTPH002 command. Creating one needs the recipient's public key; restoring or opening one needs the matching KTPH004privateKTPH005 key, and KTPH003 may ask for its passphrase.
The following sensitive and security-related data is stored in KTPH000; secret values are encrypted, while public verification material is not:
SSH key paths and encrypted passphrases
Connection passwords (inline) and key passphrases (if not using SSH key management)
Trusted public host keys for interactive Terminal, SFTP, and Mosh bootstrap connections
Scheduler sudo passwords and archive passwords; journal entries redact KorTTY-managed secrets
Master password hash (PBKDF2, 310,000 iterations) and salt
Remembered master password for the optional auto-login
Obfuscated only — not encrypted; owner-only file permissions
AI profile API keys, translation API keys, optional Hugging Face token
The open windows and tabs, with the ids of their saved connections and the folder each local shell was in; no passwords, keys or screen text
Not encrypted; owner-only file permissions, not part of backups
Only when KTPH000restoring the outputKTPH001 is switched on (off by default): the newest output of each terminal pane, which can hold anything a terminal showed

AES-256-GCM with the master-password key; never written while the vault is locked, owner-only, not part of backups, deleted when the master password changes, a backup is restored or the option is turned off

korTTY does not rewrite these files in place: a save goes to a temporary file in KTPH000 that is then renamed over the old file, for the connections, credentials, SSH keys, scheduled jobs and KTPH001 after flushing it to the disk, so a crash, a full disk or a killed process leaves the previous version intact. On macOS and Linux, korTTY keeps KTPH002 at KTPH003 and writes KTPH004, KTPH005, KTPH006, KTPH007 and KTPH008 owner-only (KTPH009), also when an older version left them readable by other users; on Windows they are protected by the permissions of your user profile.

A data file with connections, credentials, SSH or GPG keys, environments, themes or scheduled jobs that korTTY cannot parse at startup is moved aside as KTPH000 without changing it, korTTY continues without its content, and a notice lists the moved files; the next save writes a fresh file. A file that cannot be read at all, for example while a virus scanner or another program holds it or while a network home directory is unreachable, stays where it is and korTTY does not save over it for the rest of the session; the notice lists it separately. KTPH001 is never moved aside, because without it korTTY would treat the profile as new and mint a new salt: if it is damaged, unlocking fails with an error that names the file, and you restore it from a backup.

Selected terminal text sent to AI services can contain sensitive information such as credentials, hostnames, file paths, stack traces, or operational details. Before a selection goes to a profile other than an integrated model or a trusted local endpoint, korTTY masks the connection's password, your organization's replacement rules and well-known secret formats such as private keys, access tokens and passwords in URLs with KTPH000 (see KTPH001Masking secrets before sendingKTPH002). That masking is pattern-based and misses secrets in other formats, so for sensitive data still prefer an integrated local GGUF model, or verify that you trust the remote endpoint before sending anything.
Use a strong, unique master password (at least 12 characters, mix of upper/lowercase, numbers, symbols).
Keep private key files protected with a passphrase.
Copy keys to KTPH000 for inclusion in encrypted backups; keys left in their original locations are only referenced and must be migrated separately.
Limit key file permissions (e.g., KTPH000). Copies in KTPH001 are made owner-only automatically.

Verify a first-use host-key fingerprint through a trusted channel before accepting it. Treat a changed-key warning as a possible server rebuild, DNS error, or man-in-the-middle attack and investigate instead of reconnecting repeatedly. Use KTPH000Review and Replace…KTPH001 only after the server administrator has confirmed the new fingerprint.

KTPH000Host-key PinningKTPH001: Host keys are pinned by default for unattended SSH/SFTP/Rsync jobs to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. These connection-ID pins are intentionally separate from the normalized endpoint pins used by interactive Terminal/SFTP sessions.
KTPH001Sudo PasswordsKTPH002: Scheduler sudo passwords are encrypted and stored in KTPH000.
KTPH000Journal RedactionKTPH001: Job journal entries redact KorTTY-managed secrets before persistence (redacted mode is the default; full mode stores unredacted output).
Always encrypt backups using either password-protected ZIP or GPG encryption.
Store backup files in a secure location.
Test restore procedures periodically to ensure backups are usable.
API keys for AI endpoints are encrypted with your master password.
The optional Hugging Face token is encrypted with the master password and is used only for approved model search/download requests to the trusted Hugging Face host.

Each integrated KTPH000 binds only to KTPH001 on a random port and requires a generated local API key. Offline mode is mandatory; web UI, agent, UI MCP proxy, slot endpoint, and inherited server-option overrides are disabled.

GGUF downloads require an immutable repository revision and exact SHA-256 metadata. Runtime indexes require an Ed25519 signature, and every runtime ZIP is checked against its signed size and SHA-256 before safe extraction. Official application builds embed only the public runtime-channel trust root; a missing or invalid key fails closed before any update request, while the signing private key remains isolated in the human-dispatched promotion workflow.

Signed runtime withdrawals are durable and fail closed. A verified index adds withdrawn runtime and installation IDs to KTPH000, marks each installed package, clears a matching active pointer, stops its sidecars, removes it from healthy rollback history, and quarantines affected model bindings. The installer and process launcher both reject those packages, including after an interrupted update. Notification-only checks enforce a withdrawal without silently installing the offered replacement; KTPH001OffKTPH002 makes no index request and therefore learns no new withdrawal until an explicit or enabled check.

A newly activated runtime is not promoted to healthy history merely because its bounded KTPH000 check passed. It remains pending until the first real GGUF-backed authenticated API start succeeds; that start failing removes the candidate and restores/rebinds the newest healthy non-revoked package when one exists.

Model recommendations and automatic prompt-family detection can refresh from a separate Ed25519-signed HTTPS catalog. The last valid cache is re-verified before use, and a monotonic sequence rejects signed older replays or equal-sequence version collisions before an atomic high-water update. Without the independent catalog public key, korTTY trusts neither network nor cache data and falls back to the built-in bootstrap. Production catalog and runtime signing are restricted to their main-branch, reviewer-protected GitHub environments; application builds receive only the public trust roots.

AI profile configuration is stored locally; only your reviewed terminal selection or prompt is sent to the chosen service, with recognized secrets in the selection masked. Embedded inference stays on this computer.

Knowledge-store scanning follows a fixed text allowlist, validates content, refuses symbolic links, and presents a preview. Only bounded retrieved excerpts, not the complete knowledge store, enter the model prompt. Those excerpts stay local for integrated/loopback profiles but leave the computer when an explicitly assigned cloud profile handles the request; knowledge-store roles and persisted profile assignments are the user's disclosure authorization.
Remote Qdrant knowledge stores require HTTPS; plain HTTP is accepted only for loopback, and the optional API key remains vault-protected.
Internet access is disabled by default for AI profiles; enable only when needed.
Snippet AI actions never use internet access, even if the profile has it enabled.
The fixed snippet/workflow KTPH000DiagramKTPH001 request never receives knowledge-store excerpts, even when the profile has stores attached — the diagram prompt is built from the source alone.

To change your master password (which re-encrypts all stored secrets with a new derivation):
Enter the new master password twice.

Every master-password-protected secret is automatically re-encrypted with the new key: connection and jump-server passwords, SSH-key passphrases, stored credentials, AI-profile API keys and the global AI/translation/Hugging Face keys, RAG store secrets, and JobScheduler sudo/archive passwords. The change is staged — the new password only takes over once every store has migrated, so an error part-way through leaves the old password in effect. Individual secrets that cannot be migrated are left untouched, counted in the result message, and noted in the log; re-enter those manually.
